title: AWS GuardDuty → Splunk SIEM: Real-Time Cloud Threat Detection Pipeline
description: A production-style, event-driven SIEM ingestion pipeline that streams AWS GuardDuty findings into Splunk using S3 and SQS, with SOC-ready dashboards and real-time threat visibility.
long_description:
Built a real-world, event-driven SIEM pipeline to ingest AWS GuardDuty findings into Splunk using industry-standard cloud architecture.

The project implements a near real-time detection flow where GuardDuty findings are exported to S3, pushed via S3 event notifications into SQS, and consumed by the Splunk Add-on for AWS for indexing and analysis.

Key outcomes include:
- Reliable, scalable ingestion with SQS buffering and DLQ support
- Normalized GuardDuty data indexed into Splunk (aws_guardduty)
- SOC-ready dashboards with KPIs, live findings feed, timelines, and a global threat map
- No manual uploads, no cron jobs, no polling scripts

This project focuses on blue-team visibility, detection engineering, and SOC-grade observability rather than attack simulation.

title: UNIFIED HYBRID SIEM ARCHITECTURE WITH CLOUD - LOCAL HONEYPOTS AND ANALYST DRIVEN AUTOMATION

long_description:

The system centralizes threat detection, analysis, and response across hybrid enterprise environments through Azure Sentinel, delivering improved detection efficacy, minimized response times, and enhanced analyst productivity.

Performance metrics demonstrate significant improvements over traditional SIEM deployments, with 96.2% detection accuracy and sub-5-second automated response times.

Key Capabilities & Innovations:
🔐 Dual Honeypot Architecture: Deployed RDP and SMB honeypots on Windows 10 and Azure to detect brute-force attempts and exploit activity. All logs stream to Azure Sentinel for centralized analysis.
📁 Real-Time File Integrity Monitoring (FIM): Developed a Node.js FIM tool that uses SHA-256 hashing to monitor unauthorized changes in sensitive directories. Alerts are pushed instantly to Azure Log Analytics.
🧠 Machine Learning Threat Detection: Leveraged KQL and Azure Sentinel’s built-in ML capabilities to detect geolocation anomalies, unusual login patterns, and potential lateral movements across the network.
⚡ Automated Incident Response: Integrated Azure Logic Apps to trigger playbooks that isolate infected systems, block malicious IPs, and notify analysts—executing actions within 5 seconds of detection.
📊 SOC CSV Analyzer Pro: Built a Streamlit + Python-based tool for security analysts to visualize and analyze log files. Features include statistical summaries, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, heatmaps, and PDF report generation.

Performance & Results:
✅ 96.2% detection accuracy in simulated ransomware and RDP attack environments
✅ <5 seconds average automated response time
✅ 4.2% false positive rate after ML tuning
✅ 1,000+ events per second supported under stress
✅ 65% reduction in analyst log review time

Technology Stack:
Azure Sentinel, Logic Apps, Node.js, Python, Streamlit, PowerShell, Docker, GitHub Actions, KQL, MITRE ATT&CK, Windows 10, Azure Cloud

SentinelX is not just a project, it’s a working vision of what modern, intelligent, and responsive SIEM solution!

title: AI-Powered Threat Detection Pipeline using AWS GuardDuty, Lambda & Amazon Bedrock - Full Walkthrough & Technical Breakdown
description: This project involved designing and deploying a fully automated cloud-based threat detection pipeline using AWS-native services combined with generative AI. The primary objective was to build a real-time monitoring system that listens to GuardDuty findings, analyzes them using Amazon Bedrock’s large language models (LLMs), maps them to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and sends structured threat intelligence alerts to a Slack workspace.
long_description:
This project involved designing and deploying a fully automated cloud-based threat detection pipeline using AWS-native services combined with generative AI. The primary objective was to build a real-time monitoring system that listens to GuardDuty findings, analyzes them using Amazon Bedrock’s large language models (LLMs), maps them to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and sends structured threat intelligence alerts to a Slack workspace.

To begin with, Amazon GuardDuty was enabled to continuously monitor AWS resources for suspicious behavior. This included brute-force SSH attacks on EC2 instances, anomalous API calls, and cryptocurrency mining activity. Once a threat was detected by GuardDuty, an EventBridge rule forwarded the finding directly to an AWS Lambda function. This function served as the central analysis engine in the pipeline.

The Lambda function, written in Python, parsed the incoming GuardDuty JSON payload, extracted relevant fields such as threat type, description, IP addresses, and severity score. It then used Amazon Bedrock to interpret and summarize the threat in human-readable language. The Lambda logic also mapped the finding to a relevant MITRE ATT&CK technique using a custom mapping dictionary. Based on the nature of the finding, the function determined actionable steps, such as isolating an EC2 instance or blocking specific IP addresses in security groups.

For operational visibility, the Lambda function was configured to send a structured message to a Slack channel using Slack’s incoming webhooks. The alert format included the threat type, severity score, MITRE technique, affected IP addresses, a recommended action, and a timestamp. This allowed for immediate awareness and incident triage within a team communication tool without needing to check the AWS Console.

All necessary IAM roles and policies were carefully configured to follow the principle of least privilege. The Lambda function was granted permissions to invoke Bedrock models, write logs to CloudWatch, and be triggered by EventBridge. Additional logging and error handling mechanisms ensured that failures in any part of the pipeline would be logged and visible for troubleshooting.

A major challenge in this project was ensuring that real (not simulated) GuardDuty findings were properly triggered. To achieve this, the project included generating real-world SSH brute-force attempts against a deliberately exposed EC2 instance. This verified that the detection, analysis, and alerting pipeline worked end to end in a live environment. Debugging IAM misconfigurations, Slack integration issues, and proper parsing of GuardDuty payloads took several hours of iteration and testing, but the outcome was a reliable and reusable security automation workflow.

This project demonstrates hands-on proficiency in building serverless architectures on AWS, applying LLMs for cybersecurity automation, integrating cloud detection tools with communication platforms, and working with real-time security event data.

You can read the full technical breakdown, implementation walkthrough, and see all supporting screenshots in the Medium article linked below.

title: Cloud-Based Load Balancing and SDN-Powered Adaptive Video Streaming
description: A pretty solid project where I combined cloud infrastructure and software-defined networking into something actually functional and measurable.
long_description:
A pretty solid project where I combined cloud infrastructure and software-defined networking into something actually functional and measurable.

Set up a fully automated load balancer on AWS using Docker, NGINX, PHP, and MySQL. The system handled backend traffic with zero downtime and showed an 18.6 percent increase in throughput under load. Wrote a script to deploy everything in one go, no manual setup, no surprises.

On the other side, I built a video streaming testbed using Mininet and DASH.js, controlled by an SDN controller (OpenDaylight). The player adapted to real-time network changes like packet loss and bandwidth drops. I customized the DASH player to track bitrate shifts, buffer levels, and resolution changes, all in real time.

Everything was built from scratch. No templates. Every part was scripted and tested under real conditions.

This was about solving real infrastructure problems using the tools that power today’s internet. On to the next!

title: Security Operations - OSSEC HIDS: Detecting the EternalBlue Exploitation
description: This project focused on using OSSEC HIDS (Host-Based Intrusion Detection System) to detect and respond to the well-known EternalBlue (MS17-010) vulnerability exploitation. The attack was simulated in a controlled lab environment, and OSSEC was configured to monitor, log, and generate alerts for suspicious activities related to the exploit. This hands-on exercise highlighted the importance of proactive monitoring in cybersecurity defense and demonstrated how OSSEC can identify critical Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in real time.
long_description:
Overview:
This project focused on using OSSEC HIDS (Host-Based Intrusion Detection System) to detect and respond to the well-known EternalBlue (MS17-010) vulnerability exploitation. The attack was simulated in a controlled lab environment, and OSSEC was configured to monitor, log, and generate alerts for suspicious activities related to the exploit. This hands-on exercise highlighted the importance of proactive monitoring in cybersecurity defense and demonstrated how OSSEC can identify critical Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in real time.

Key Achievements:
Lab Environment Setup:
Designed a controlled environment with Kali Linux (attacker), Windows 7 SP1 (target), and Ubuntu (monitoring system running OSSEC).
Configured OSSEC server and agent, and deployed OSSEC Web UI for real-time visualization of alerts and logs.
OSSEC HIDS Configuration and Monitoring:
Installed and configured OSSEC on the Ubuntu monitoring system, including agent communication and alert settings.
Monitored the attack process using OSSEC, detecting unauthorized user account creation, group membership changes, and suspicious SMB traffic associated with EternalBlue exploitation.
EternalBlue Exploitation:
Used Metasploit to exploit the EternalBlue vulnerability (MS17-010) on the Windows 7 target system.
Simulated a real-world attack by gaining unauthorized access, creating user accounts, and escalating privileges on the target system.
OSSEC detected and logged these activities, raising alerts for key events, including user account creation and privilege escalation.
Intrusion Detection and Response:
OSSEC flagged critical alerts related to unauthorized account creation (Rule ID: 18110) and changes in group membership (Rule ID: 18223).
Analyzed the alerts in the OSSEC Web UI and identified the attack patterns in real-time, demonstrating the value of proactive host-based monitoring.
Recommendations and Mitigations:
Identified key vulnerabilities related to SMB traffic and weak access control policies.
Recommended patching systems with the latest security updates (e.g., MS17-010), strengthening password policies, and using network segmentation to limit the spread of attacks.
Suggested integrating OSSEC with a SIEM tool (e.g., Splunk or Azure Sentinel) for enhanced log aggregation and incident response.
Skills and Technologies:
Tools Used: OSSEC HIDS, Metasploit, Kali Linux, Windows 7 SP1, Ubuntu, OSSEC Web UI.
Key Skills: Host-based intrusion detection, vulnerability exploitation, incident detection, log analysis, system monitoring, real-time alerting, security patching, and vulnerability mitigation.
Methodology: Configured and deployed OSSEC for real-time attack monitoring. Used Metasploit for the exploitation of EternalBlue, and analyzed OSSEC logs to detect and respond to the attack, following best practices for intrusion detection and response.
Outcome:
The project demonstrated effective detection of a critical vulnerability (EternalBlue) using OSSEC HIDS, showcasing its capabilities in identifying key Indicators of Compromise in real time. It also emphasized the need for continuous monitoring and proactive defense strategies, such as integrating OSSEC with SIEM solutions and enhancing system patching practices. The project provided valuable insights for improving cybersecurity defenses and solidified the role of HIDS in detecting sophisticated attack vectors like EternalBlue.

Tools used include FTK Imager, Wireshark, Volatility, and Autopsy. Delivered actionable recommendations to strengthen cybersecurity practices and prevent future breaches.

This project was part of a coursework requirement for the PUSL3133 module on Digital Forensics & Malware Analysis. The investigation revolved around an unauthorized data transfer incident at ABC Company. A digital forensic approach was applied to uncover the details of the breach, determine its scope, and recommend mitigation strategies.

Key Objectives:
Quantify the Data Loss: Identify the type and volume of data compromised to evaluate organizational risks.
Preserve Digital Evidence: Collect and maintain evidence to ensure its admissibility in legal or organizational proceedings.
Identify the Culprit: Pinpoint whether the breach was internal or external, using activity logs, email analysis, and network traffic monitoring.
Enhance Security Measures: Suggest immediate and long-term solutions to improve ABC Company’s cybersecurity posture.
Key Steps and Techniques:
Digital Evidence Acquisition:
Utilized forensic tools such as FTK Imager to create bit-by-bit forensic images.
Maintained the chain of custody by documenting hash values, timestamps, and tools used.
Analyzed stored email data, suspect files, and network logs.
Email Analysis:
Used tools like Autopsy, Kernel PST Viewer, and MXToolbox to investigate suspicious emails.
Conducted header analysis to detect spoofing attempts and email authentication failures (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).
Identified hidden data using steganography detection in attachments.
Network Analysis:
Examined anomalies in email headers and correlated them with network activity using MXToolbox.
Identified unauthorized access from suspicious IPs.
Justification of Tools:
Each tool was selected based on its ability to handle email metadata analysis, network traffic correlation, and forensic imaging.
Findings and Recommendations:
Discovered spoofed email activity leading to data exfiltration.
Identified gaps in ABC Company’s email authentication protocols.
Recommended implementing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC standards, advanced network monitoring, and employee training to mitigate future risks.
Challenges Overcome:
Worked with limited network traffic data (PCAP files were unavailable).
Ensured data integrity and legal compliance while preserving the chain of custody.
Coordinated analysis across various forensic tools to achieve comprehensive results.
Outcome: The project successfully uncovered the details of the unauthorized data transfer, identified potential risks, and provided a roadmap for improving ABC Company’s cybersecurity defenses. This practical experience reinforced skills in email forensics, network analysis, and evidence handling while adhering to legal and organizational standards.

description: A File Integrity Monitor that allows users to track down real-time insights on file changes. Developed using PowerShell scripting. Whether you're a cybersecurity enthusiast or just curious about maintaining data security, this tool is for you.
long_description:
A File Integrity Monitor that allows users to track down real-time insights on file changes. Developed using PowerShell scripting. Welcome to the File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) System repository! This tool helps you monitor the integrity of your files, safeguarding your digital assets against unauthorized changes. Whether you're a cybersecurity enthusiast or just curious about maintaining data security, this tool is for you.

📋 How does it work? It's simple! The system has two modes:

1️⃣ Collecting Baseline: Start by collecting a baseline of your files' hash values. This essentially captures the current state of your files and their hashes. If you spot any unexpected changes in the future, you'll have something to compare against.

2️⃣ Monitoring Mode: Once you have your baseline, switch to the monitoring mode. The system continuously scans your files, recalculates their hash values, and compares them to the baseline. If a file is created, modified, or deleted, you'll be notified in real-time, thanks to color-coded alerts that I've included.

🟢 Green: New files added.
🔵 Blue: Files remain unchanged.
🟣 Magenta: Files have been modified.
🔴 Dark Red: Files have been deleted.

📁 Getting Started: You can grab the code for this FIM system from my GitHub repository. Clone it, set it up, and run it in your own environment. The repository includes step-by-step instructions to guide you through the setup process.
